channel.title: Surveys on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Surveys on Best of AI

item.title: AppFollow
item.description:
Reviews can be tagged, translated, and routed to the right team. AI-assisted replies and review summaries help with high volume. Its keyword and competitor tracking supports store listing updates.

Subscription pricing depends on app count and features. It connects to tools like Slack and Jira so feedback reaches product teams.

AppTweak and Sensor Tower are alternatives. AppFollow suits app store optimizers and support teams that manage reviews.

item.title: AppTweak
item.description:
Marketers use it to find keyword ideas, check search volume estimates, and monitor changes in ratings and reviews. AI features suggest metadata and summarize review themes. It covers Apple App Store and Google Play.

Plans are subscription based. Results depend on store algorithms, which change.

AppFollow and Sensor Tower are alternatives. AppTweak suits app store optimizers and growth teams.

item.title: Medallia
item.description:
Teams analyze comments with text analytics to find themes and sentiment. Alerts route unhappy customers to staff for follow-up. Dashboards track satisfaction by location, product, or channel.

Enterprise pricing, with implementation help typically needed.

Qualtrics is the main alternative. Medallia suits customer experience managers at large organizations.

item.title: Prolific
item.description:
Researchers set screening criteria, such as age, country, or language, and pay participants for their time. Participants are vetted, and the platform tracks quality. It connects with survey tools like Qualtrics and experiment builders.

Pricing is based on participant payments plus a platform fee. Samples are online volunteers, so results may not represent the general population.

MTurk and CloudResearch are alternatives. Prolific suits behavioral scientists and academic researchers.

item.title: Sensor Tower
item.description:
App publishers use it to benchmark competitors, find keywords, and study how top apps present themselves. App store optimization features show how listings rank for search terms. Reports cover categories, regions, and trends.

Figures are estimates, not official numbers, so they are best used for relative comparison. Pricing is custom and aimed at businesses.

AppTweak and AppFollow are alternatives. Sensor Tower suits app marketers and product teams.

item.title: FullStory
item.description:
FullStory lets teams see how real people use their websites and apps. It captures sessions, which can be replayed like a video of the user’s screen, and detects signals such as rage clicks, dead clicks, and error clicks that suggest frustration. Searching across sessions helps teams find all users affected by a particular bug or those who abandoned a checkout step, instead of guessing from numbers alone.

Beyond replays, it offers analytics such as funnels, heatmaps, and journey maps, and tools for tying issues to revenue impact. AI features summarize sessions and surface patterns, so teams don’t have to watch hundreds of recordings, and help prioritize the problems that matter most. Privacy controls mask sensitive information, and integrations send findings to engineering and support tools like Jira and Slack.

item.title: Microsoft Clarity
item.description:
Clarity shows how people really use a website. A snippet of code installed on the site captures sessions, which can be replayed like a video, along with heatmaps that show where visitors click and how far they scroll. It automatically flags signs of frustration, including rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling, and JavaScript errors, so teams can focus on pages where users struggle.

AI features add convenience. Copilot summarizes many sessions to surface common issues and gives answers to questions about user behavior, and filters let you segment by device, country, and traffic source. Clarity also offers insights on how AI chatbots and search drive traffic to a site. It integrates with Google Analytics, Microsoft Advertising, and platforms such as Shopify and WordPress.

item.title: SurveyMonkey
item.description:
SurveyMonkey is one of the best-known survey tools. Users create surveys with a drag-and-drop builder, choose from templates for customer satisfaction, employee engagement, market research, and events, and share them by link, email, or embedding. Question logic, branching, and randomization allow more sophisticated designs, and responses appear in real time with charts and filters.

AI features aim to make surveys better and analysis quicker. The assistant can build a survey from a description, suggest improved wording to avoid bias, and analyze open-ended responses by identifying themes and sentiment. A panel service lets researchers purchase responses from target audiences, and integrations connect results to tools like Salesforce, Slack, and Tableau.

item.title: Muck Rack
item.description:
Muck Rack is a public relations platform. PR professionals search its database to find journalists who cover a topic, see what they have written recently, and build media lists. They send pitches and track responses, and the platform monitors news to show where their company or clients are mentioned.

Reporting tools measure coverage by reach and sentiment, and dashboards show how campaigns perform. AI features summarize articles, suggest journalists, and help draft pitches, saving time on research and writing. The company also publishes research about the relationship between journalists and PR.

item.title: Glassbox
item.description:
Glassbox captures user sessions on digital properties. Teams can replay a visit to see what a customer clicked, where they hesitated, and what errors they hit. Heatmaps summarize click and scroll behavior across many sessions, pointing to confusing pages or broken flows.

The platform adds analytics and detection. Journey analysis shows where users leave a funnel, and automatic detection flags frustration signals such as repeated clicks. It has features for regulated industries like banking, including data masking so that sensitive information is not stored. The company has expanded through acquisitions into areas like anomaly detection.

item.title: Talkwalker
item.description:
Talkwalker monitors the public conversation about brands and topics. Users set up searches, and the platform collects posts, articles, forums, and broadcast mentions from around the world, then analyzes volume, sentiment, and who is talking. Alerts flag spikes that may signal a crisis or opportunity.

Image and video recognition detect logos in pictures even when the brand name is not written, and AI summarizes themes and trends. Marketing and communications teams use the findings to measure campaigns, track competitors, and shape messaging, and a generative assistant helps analysts query the data.

item.title: Meltwater
item.description:
Meltwater is a media monitoring and social listening platform. Users set up searches for brand names, competitors, and topics, and the system collects mentions from news sites, blogs, social networks, forums, and broadcast sources, with alerts and dashboards.

Analytics show volume, sentiment, and reach, and AI highlights trends and unusual spikes, such as the start of a negative story. Tools for PR teams include media databases for finding journalists, and distribution of press releases. Reports demonstrate the impact of campaigns.

item.title: Qualtrics
item.description:
Qualtrics is an experience management platform. Organizations use it to run customer satisfaction surveys, product research, brand studies, and employee engagement programs. A powerful survey builder handles complex logic, and results flow into dashboards segmented by customer, team, or time.

AI features turn feedback into action. They analyze comments for sentiment and themes, spot issues as they emerge, predict which customers may leave, and suggest next steps. The platform also pulls in data from support calls, reviews, and social media.

item.title: Attention Insight
item.description: Attention Insight offers an inexpensive shortcut to a classic design question: will anyone notice this? Upload a screenshot, ad, packaging mockup, or video, and its AI produces a heatmap of the areas likely to draw the eye in the first few seconds. The model is trained on eye-tracking data, so the predictions approximate what real viewers would do. It returns results in seconds, which makes it practical to compare several versions of a design.

item.title: Brandwatch
item.description:
Brandwatch is used by marketing, communications, and research teams to understand what people say online. It collects posts and mentions from social networks, news sites, forums, blogs, and reviews, and lets analysts build searches to track a brand, a competitor, a campaign, or a topic. Dashboards show volume over time, sentiment, demographics, top influencers, and emerging themes, which helps with campaign measurement, crisis monitoring, and product feedback.

AI plays a role in making sense of the data. Language models classify sentiment and topics, group conversations into themes, summarize large sets of posts, and answer questions about the findings in natural language. Image recognition finds logos in pictures posted without any text. Alerts warn teams when mentions spike, and the social management side supports publishing and responding to messages from one place.

item.title: CB Insights
item.description:
CB Insights tracks the innovation economy. Its database covers private companies, funding rounds, investors, acquisitions, patents, and news, and analysts and algorithms turn that into research on market trends. Corporate strategy teams, investors, and consultants use it to understand which sectors are growing and who the major players are.

Features include company profiles, market maps, forecasts of company outcomes, and an AI assistant that answers questions from the platform’s data and research. Alerts and newsletters keep subscribers up to date, and tools support building lists of companies matching specific criteria.

item.title: Crimson Hexagon
item.description: Crimson Hexagon was a consumer insights company that analyzed social media, news, forums, and review data at large scale. It was known for its ForSight platform and for machine learning that classified posts by sentiment and topic with accuracy that researchers could tune. Market researchers, agencies, and brands used it to track what people said about products and campaigns, and its archive of historical social data was a draw for studying trends over time.

item.title: Crunchbase
item.description:
Crunchbase is a widely used database about startups and private companies. Users look up a company to see its founders, funding history, investors, and news, or search for companies by industry, location, and stage. Investors, salespeople, and researchers use it to find targets and track activity.

Predictive features add forward-looking signals. AI models estimate which companies are likely to raise money, grow, or be acquired, and alerts notify users when relevant events happen. Lists and integrations send data into CRMs for prospecting.

item.title: Hotjar AI
item.description:
Hotjar helps teams see what visitors actually do on a site. Heatmaps show where people click, move, and scroll, session recordings replay individual visits, and on-page surveys and feedback widgets ask visitors what they think. Together they reveal confusing layouts, broken elements, and places where people give up, which complements numbers from analytics tools that show what happened but not why.

AI cuts down the time it takes to find insights. Instead of watching hundreds of recordings, teams can get automatic summaries of sessions, highlights of common frustrations, and analysis of open-ended survey responses grouped into themes. This helps designers, product managers, and marketers decide what to fix first. Funnels and trends let you see where users drop out, and integrations send findings to tools like Slack, Jira, and HubSpot.

item.title: Maze
item.description:
Maze helps product teams learn from users. Designers import a prototype from Figma, set tasks for participants, and share a link to run a test that records clicks, paths, and success rates. Surveys, card sorts, and interview studies are supported as well, and a panel service can recruit participants.

AI speeds up analysis. It transcribes sessions, pulls out themes and quotes, and writes summaries of what the data shows, so teams spend less time sorting through recordings. Reports can be shared with stakeholders.

item.title: SEMrush
item.description:
Semrush bundles many marketing tools in one subscription. Users research keywords, audit websites, track rankings, analyze backlinks, spy on competitors’ traffic and ads, and plan content, all from a shared dashboard. It is widely used by agencies and in-house teams.

AI features help with writing and analysis. A writing assistant drafts and optimizes content, AI tools summarize data and suggest actions, and newer products track how brands appear in AI-generated answers from chat assistants, a growing concern for search marketers. Reports and integrations suit client work.

item.title: SimilarWeb
item.description:
Similarweb lets you look at the performance of sites you do not own. Enter a domain, and it shows estimated monthly visits, traffic sources such as search, social, and direct, top keywords, referring sites, audience demographics, and engagement metrics like time on site. Data comes from a mix of panels, partnerships, and public sources, modeled to produce estimates. This helps in benchmarking competitors and finding growth opportunities.

The platform covers more than websites. It tracks app usage and downloads, advertising, and market segments, and ranks sites within categories. Recent additions include tracking how brands and sites are cited and visited through AI chatbots, reflecting the way people increasingly use AI assistants instead of search. Investors use the data to spot trends in company performance before financial reports, and sales teams use it to find leads.

item.title: Quantilope
item.description:
Quantilope aims to let research teams run advanced studies without waiting weeks on an agency. Researchers pick from automated methods, such as concept tests, segmentation, pricing studies, and brand tracking, set up the survey, and field it to respondents from a panel. Analysis and charts are generated as data comes in.

The platform’s AI helps design studies, suggests suitable methods, writes summaries of findings, and answers questions about the data. Because methodologies are built in, non-specialists can run studies that would normally need a statistician.

item.title: Remesh
item.description:
Remesh scales the focus group. A moderator poses questions to hundreds of participants at once, and people respond in their own words and then rate each other’s answers, so the group quickly reveals where opinions agree and differ. Responses are analyzed as they arrive.

AI clusters comments into themes, summarizes sentiment, and highlights segments by demographic. Researchers use it for message testing, employee listening, public policy input, and product research. A single session can produce depth and breadth that would take many interviews.

item.title: Competitor Analyzer
item.description:
Competitor Analyzer helps small teams keep an eye on the market without a full-time analyst. You enter your competitors, and the tool watches their websites, social accounts, content, and in some cases pricing, then summarizes what changed in a weekly digest. The aim is to save the time spent checking sites by hand.

Typical uses include spotting a rival’s new feature or campaign, tracking pricing changes, and gathering material for positioning. AI summaries make the digests quick to read and highlight notable changes. The tool is positioned as simpler and cheaper than enterprise competitive intelligence platforms.

item.title: Cresh
item.description:
Cresh is built for early-stage business research. A user describes an idea or market, and several AI agents search sources, gather information, and assemble a report covering competitors, market size, customer needs, and risks. The aim is a fast first pass that would otherwise require manual searching.

Founders use it to test ideas before investing time, and analysts use it to build starting briefs. Reports from AI research tools can contain errors and unsupported claims, so figures and sources should be checked before decisions or investor materials rely on them.
